title: Lecturers’ perceptions of the influence of AI on a blended learning approach in a South African higher education institution
extended_summary:
This paper examines how lecturers perceive the influence of artificial intelligence on blended learning in a South African higher education institution. The central problem is the limited understanding of lecturers’ views on how AI can enhance blended teaching and learning, what challenges arise during implementation, and what kinds of support are needed for successful integration. The study is framed by the SAMR model (Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition) to interpret different levels of AI integration in teaching practice.

The researchers conducted a qualitative single-case study using semi-structured focus group interviews and document analysis. The approach focused on how lecturers were already using AI within blended learning rather than testing a controlled intervention. Reported uses of AI included answering student queries, generating customized learning materials and assessments, enabling translation across languages, providing real-time feedback, supporting interactive activities, and automating some administrative tasks. The document analysis was used to corroborate lecturers’ descriptions with examples from module sites, such as adaptive quizzes, AI-generated case studies, automated feedback, and translation tools.

The study involved 15 lecturers from the College of Education at one South African higher education institution. Although the direct participants were lecturers, the educational context included their students in blended courses, and the paper discusses perceived effects on student engagement, communication, personalization, and learning support. The setting was a blended higher education environment combining face-to-face and online instruction.

The main conclusions are that lecturers generally viewed AI as beneficial for blended learning, especially for personalization, communication, quick feedback, adaptive assessment, and broader access to learning materials. At the same time, they identified substantial barriers, including resistance to change, time constraints, uneven student access to technology, ethical and privacy concerns, limited infrastructure, and the need to balance AI with traditional pedagogy. The paper concludes that successful AI-enabled blended learning requires strong institutional support, professional development, management backing, reliable internet and technological infrastructure, technical support, and dedicated time for lecturers to learn and implement AI effectively.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic artificial intelligence tools and functions in blended learning environments, including chatbots, adaptive assessment, automated feedback, translation, and AI-supported content generation; no specific named product is identified.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as lecturers' reported uses and perceptions of AI integrated into blended learning in a South African higher education institution, including answering student queries, facilitating discussion, generating customized materials and assessments, translation, automated grading, and real-time feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative single-case study of 15 lecturers, all participants reported that AI was useful in blended learning, especially for saving time, automating some administrative tasks, generating materials and assessments, and providing faster responses to student queries. Seven lecturers specifically described AI as streamlining administrative tasks and enabling adaptation of teaching based on student performance data, but no effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Lecturers' perceptions from semi-structured focus group interviews and document analysis regarding efficiency, automation, and instructional support

findings.finding_summary: The study found that successful AI integration in blended learning was perceived to depend on institutional support, management backing, professional development, reliable infrastructure, internet connectivity, and dedicated time. At the same time, lecturers reported major implementation barriers including resistance to change (12 lecturers), time constraints (all participants), digital divide concerns (8 lecturers), and ethical/privacy concerns, indicating mixed institutional readiness rather than direct performance effects.
findings.measure: Lecturers' reported implementation challenges and support needs for AI-integrated blended learning

findings.finding_summary: Lecturers perceived AI as improving blended learning through personalized support, instant feedback, adaptive assessments, and increased engagement. Nine lecturers highlighted the value of immediate AI feedback, and document analysis confirmed examples of AI-supported scenario feedback, adaptive quizzes, automated grading, and translation support, but no direct student achievement data or standardized outcome measures were reported.
findings.measure: Lecturers' perceptions and document-analysis evidence related to student engagement, personalized learning, feedback, and learning support

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative single-case study based on interviews and document analysis with 15 lecturers, not an experimental or quasi-experimental evaluation of student outcomes. The methodology is clearly described, but evidence remains perception-based and non-causal.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports generally positive perceived benefits of AI integration, but impact is unclear because no effect sizes, comparative analyses, or direct student outcome data are provided. Reported findings are mainly qualitative perceptions mixed with implementation challenges.
